report:
## Conclusion

The claim that **capsaicin treats breast cancer in humans is not supported by current evidence**. While capsaicin shows promising anti-cancer activity in laboratory and animal studies, no human clinical trials have demonstrated it as an effective treatment for breast cancer.

**What the evidence shows:**

- **In vitro studies** demonstrate that capsaicin can inhibit proliferation and induce apoptosis (programmed cell death) in breast cancer cell lines such as MCF-7 and MDA-MB-231, acting through multiple signaling pathways including cell-cycle arrest and modulation of oncogenes and tumor-suppressor genes ([Dovepress](https://www.dovepress.com/capsaicin-inhibits-proliferation-and-induces-apoptosis-in-breast-cance-peer-reviewed-fulltext-article-DDDT); [Anticancer Research](https://ar.iiarjournals.org/content/36/3/837)).

- **Animal studies** have shown reduced tumor size, but these findings have not yet translated to proven human therapies ([PMC](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6274000/)).

- **No human clinical trials** have tested capsaicin as a breast cancer treatment. The only capsaicin-related clinical trials in breast cancer patients involve high-concentration capsaicin patches for managing **postsurgical neuropathic pain**, not for treating the cancer itself ([MDPI/Cancers](https://www.mdpi.com/2072-6694/17/2/313)).

- **Snopes** explicitly fact-checked this claim and concluded that while capsaicin "does have cancer fighting properties in the lab, its use as an anti-cancer therapy in humans is far from certain," citing challenges such as drug delivery to tumor sites ([Snopes](https://www.snopes.com/fact-check/spicy-peppers-breast-cancer/)).

**Bottom line:** Capsaicin is a promising candidate for future research, but it has not been proven to treat breast cancer in humans. Anyone considering it as a therapy should consult an oncologist.
